title: The Food Laws
lead: The laws of which animals Israel may eat (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14), with the ban on blood (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17). They remain the basis of Jewish kashrut; the New Testament's handling of them (Mark 7:19; Acts 10; Romans 14) marks a major parting of Jewish and Christian practice.

sections.b: Genesis gives all animals to Noah for food, with blood forbidden (Genesis 9:3–4), while still knowing clean and unclean kinds (Genesis 7:2). Exodus forbids meat torn by wild animals (Exodus 22:31) and boiling a young goat in its mother's milk (Exodus 23:19). Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 give the full lists, and Leviticus 17 the ban on blood. Daniel and his friends refuse the king's food (Daniel 1:8), and in the Maccabean crisis Jews died rather than eat pork (2 Maccabees 6–7). In the New Testament, Mark 7:19 says Jesus made all foods clean, Peter's vision (Acts 10) and the Jerusalem council (Acts 15) apply the question to Gentiles, and Paul treats food as a matter of conscience and love (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8–10).
